title: Bowling For Votes

jokes.text: Focus group participant says Leslie is 'aggressively short' and 'throwing it in my face'
jokes.setup: Focus group is asked for general impressions of the candidate
jokes.punchline: 'Aggressively short almost. It's like she's throwing it in my face.' — treating height as a personal affront is a surreal escalation
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'kinda short' to 'aggressively short' to 'throwing it in my face' is absurdly funny because the logic is internally consistent but completely irrational. Good economy and originality; loses points because it's not character-specific to Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The focus group said I need to be more vulnerable, so I'm just going to come out and say it: I have feelings about myself.

jokes.text: Leslie immediately writes a note to herself to tell Ron to tell Ben how good she is at bowling — while claiming she's not obsessing
jokes.setup: Ben tells Leslie not to get obsessed over one comment. She agrees she won't.
jokes.punchline: She is immediately, visibly writing a note to engineer a third-party endorsement of her bowling ability
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the irony is instantaneous — she hasn't even finished her sentence before contradicting it; (2) the specificity of routing the endorsement through Ron to Ben is delightfully bureaucratic and Knope-ish; (3) it also plants the 'Ask Ron' running gag. The structure is tight and the character integration is nearly perfect — this is quintessentially Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Focus Group Member
dialogue.line: She's aggressively short. Like, she chose to be that tall to spite us.

jokes.text: 'Although I once knew a Leslie, and she was just awful. So now I hate all Leslies. Would she consider changing her name?'
jokes.setup: A focus group participant says he'd actually vote for Leslie and thinks she's smart
jokes.punchline: He immediately undermines it by explaining he hates all Leslies due to one bad experience, then sincerely asks if she'd consider a name change
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist setup/punchline. The misdirection is strong — he starts positively, pivots to a ridiculous generalization, then delivers the sincere follow-up question ('Would she consider changing her name?') which escalates the absurdity. This captures Pawnee's unique brand of well-intentioned idiocy perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Cool.

jokes.text: I'VE NEVER BEEN VERY GOOD AT LETTING THINGS GO. I CAN'T TELL YOU HOW MANY TIMES A FUN TUG-OF-WAR WITH A DOG OVER A CHEW TOY TURNED CONTENTIOUS. ONE OF US ALWAYS ENDS UP MAD.
jokes.setup: Ben tells Leslie she really has to let the bowling comment go
jokes.punchline: Leslie illustrates her inability to let things go with the anecdote of a tug-of-war with a dog — with no self-awareness that this is an admission of a character flaw
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed Leslie confessional. The dog anecdote is specific and strange in exactly the right way, and the total lack of self-awareness ('one of us always ends up mad') is the perfect character beat. Only Leslie would tell this story as though it proves her point.

dialogue.speaker: Focus Group Member
dialogue.line: I'm not voting for Leslie Knope. We took a bowling compatibility test and we're not compatible bowlers.

jokes.text: Leslie has researched Derek from the focus group — knows his bowling average is 132 — 'according to the most recent available data'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to explain the real political issue behind Derek's comment; Leslie claims she did 'some research'
jokes.punchline: She knows Derek's full name AND his bowling average (132), qualified with 'according to the most recent available data' — bureaucratic precision applied to a petty obsession
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'according to the most recent available data' applied to a random guy's bowling league stats is peak Leslie Knope. It shows her obsessive, data-driven personality applied to something completely petty. The character integration is nearly perfect — only Leslie would phrase it that way. Strong structure with the escalating reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Bowling is a sport, Derek. It's in the Olympics. And Ron Swanson once told me that bowling is the only acceptable form of exercise because you can do it while eating a hot dog.

jokes.text: Leslie invokes Woodrow Wilson and Benjamin Disraeli when accused of being elitist, then immediately catches herself
jokes.setup: Ben says people think Leslie is a little elitist or intellectual. Leslie protests it's sexist.
jokes.punchline: She references two obscure historical figures from two different countries to defend herself, then mid-sentence realizes she's proving Ben's point
jokes.explanation: This joke is excellent because the self-correction happens in real time — Leslie catches herself being exactly what she's denying. The choice of Disraeli specifically (a British PM) rather than an American is the comic detail that makes it great. Only Leslie would invoke a Victorian-era British Prime Minister to prove she's relatable. The structure is clean and the self-awareness adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can't obsess over one comment about your bowling skills.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: One comment? Ben, I've already drafted a memo proposing we form a Parks Department bowling league, and I've created a seventeen-person committee to oversee it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The committee will report to a sub-committee, which will report to a oversight board, which will report directly to the City Manager.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've also prepared a PowerPoint presentation with pie charts demonstrating the health benefits of bowling.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And I'm entering the regional bowling tournament next weekend. So.

jokes.text: 'Also I'm really good at bowling.' / 'No, I don't think I believe you. Is there anyone I can ask?' / 'Yeah. Ask Ron.'
jokes.setup: The bowling event idea is proposed for legitimate political reasons
jokes.punchline: Leslie can't help redirecting to her personal bowling prowess; Ben plays along by asking for verification; she refers him to Ron
jokes.explanation: The 'Ask Ron' running gag pays off here with Ben now actively participating in the bit. The economy is excellent — the joke escalates from Leslie asserting to Ben skeptically asking to her delivering the exact punchline set up earlier. Character dynamic between Leslie and Ben is well-served.

dialogue.speaker: Focus Group Member
dialogue.line: I'd vote for Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Focus Group Member
dialogue.line: But I gotta be honest, I don't like her last name. Knope? It sounds like a sneeze. If she changed it to something like Leslie... Hopeston, I'd vote for her 100%.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I don't know, Jerry. It's Sunday night, I'm making phone calls to strangers, and you're in my house. My life couldn't be worse.'
jokes.setup: Jerry enthusiastically asks if everyone is feeling good about the phone bank
jokes.punchline: Ann lists three specific miseries culminating in Jerry's presence as the worst of all, delivered flatly
jokes.explanation: Solid Jerry-as-unwanted-presence joke. The list structure builds nicely to the punchline — Jerry's presence is ranked equal to or worse than Sunday cold-calling strangers. Functionally good, relies somewhat on the established 'Jerry is pathetic' gag that's a show-wide crutch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not good at letting things go. Like, I once mediated a custody battle between Ben and me over a dog toy. I presented a PowerPoint.

jokes.text: OH, I DON'T KNOW, JERRY. IT'S SUNDAY NIGHT, I'M MAKING PHONE CALLS TO STRANGERS, AND YOU'RE IN MY HOUSE. MY LIFE COULDN'T BE WORSE.
jokes.setup: Jerry cheerfully asks if everyone's feeling good at the phone bank
jokes.punchline: April catalogues three things — including Jerry's presence — as reasons her life couldn't be worse, delivered with complete flat affect
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for April. The list builds to 'and you're in my house' as the third, most specifically awful thing — elevating Jerry's mere presence to a life-ruining event. Classic April-hates-Jerry and perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I did my research on you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your name is Jerry.

jokes.text: 'Let's get this phone party started.' — Jerry's oblivious enthusiasm
jokes.setup: Ann has just told him his presence makes her life worse
jokes.punchline: Jerry either doesn't process the insult or chooses to ignore it and enthusiastically calls it a 'phone party'
jokes.explanation: Functional Jerry obliviousness joke. 'Phone party' is mildly amusing but this is bread-and-butter Jerry humor without a surprising twist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've been doing some research on you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What kind of research?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I looked into your bowling statistics from high school. You averaged 147 pins per game in 1998.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You investigated my bowling statistics?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I investigate the things I care about.

jokes.text: Tom cuts off April's question 'You're probably thinking, how could it possibly be fun?' with 'No one's thinking that' / 'I kinda was' / 'I was not' / 'Why are we laughing?'
jokes.setup: Tom gives a motivational speech and rhetorically asks if anyone was wondering how phone banking could be fun
jokes.punchline: April immediately contradicts him, Ann takes the opposite position, and the group laughter confuses everyone — rapid-fire deflation of Tom's big moment
jokes.explanation: Good group dynamics joke. The overlapping contradictions and the final 'Why are we laughing?' captures the chaotic ensemble energy well. Tom's deflation is well-earned. The structure of the rapid-fire back-and-forth is efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, did you really spend all weekend researching bowling techniques?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not just techniques, Ben. I cross-referenced historical bowling data with demographic trends, analyzed ball weight optimization for various wrist configurations, and I may have created a seventeen-page binder.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A seventeen-page... Leslie, we're just going bowling for fun.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fun? Ben, there is no such thing as 'just' bowling. Every frame is an opportunity for excellence.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh my God. You're serious about this.

jokes.text: Chris's talking-head confessional: 'As city manager, I play no favorites. But as a private citizen, I am free to support whomever I choose... Everybody's the best. We're all winners.'
jokes.setup: Chris declares his private support for Team Knope with dramatic legal preamble
jokes.punchline: He immediately retreats into his relentless positivity and inclusivity — undermining the competitive spirit of the declaration by saying everyone is the best and everyone wins
jokes.explanation: A reliable Chris joke format: the civic legalese preamble followed by the sunshine meltdown. The escalation from competitive ('Out of my way, suckers') back to 'we're all winners' is a nice character loop but the joke type is familiar territory for his character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This criticism is completely sexist! You wouldn't say these things about a man who was passionate and driven and had strong opinions about—wait. Oh my god. I'm being elitist right now, aren't I?

jokes.text: Leslie asks 'Do I look laid-back?' / Ben: 'You look like you're trying to look laid-back.' / 'How about now?' / 'Maybe just stand how you would normally stand.' / 'Okay. I forget now.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to appear casual and approachable at the bowling alley event
jokes.punchline: She cannot perform relaxation naturally, and when told to stand normally, reveals she has no default casual mode — she can't remember how she normally stands
jokes.explanation: The 'I forget now' punchline is the best moment — it implies Leslie's natural resting state is so wound-up that she can't access it on command. Strong character integration. The escalation from the question to her inability to perform normality is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm actually really good at bowling.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, I'm going to need to see some credentials. Maybe a bowling license, a letter of recommendation from the pins.

jokes.text: 'This bowling alley has my favorite restaurant in Pawnee.' — Ron, completely earnest
jokes.setup: Ben expresses surprise or discomfort about the bowling alley setting
jokes.punchline: Ron has no hesitation about a bowling alley having his favorite restaurant — his carnivorous, unironic appreciation for lowbrow food is absolute
jokes.explanation: Deeply Ron Swanson. The joke works because he says it with zero self-consciousness — a bowling alley restaurant is, to Ron, a legitimate and superior dining option. The character integration is near-perfect. Economy is great: one sentence does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Who should I ask about this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Me! You should ask me!

jokes.text: 'Really? You're not scared to eat here?' / 'When I eat, it is the food that is scared.'
jokes.setup: Ben questions Ron's comfort eating at a bowling alley restaurant
jokes.punchline: Ron's response reframes the dynamic — he is the apex predator, the food is prey — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is the standout line of the episode. 'When I eat, it is the food that is scared' is exceptional on every dimension: the structure subverts the expected 'no I'm not scared' response with a complete reversal of agency; the character integration is perfect (only Ron Swanson); the economy is flawless (ten words); the originality is high for a sitcom line; and it's supremely quotable. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor and arguably exceeds it. This is what an 8.5+ looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Is everybody feeling good about phone banking?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No. I'm in Hell. This is Hell. I'm being punished for something I did in a past life. There's no other explanation for why I'm here making phone calls to strangers and listening to them describe their problems.

jokes.text: Tom arrives in elaborate bowling gear — 'Tommy's new bowling swag'
jokes.setup: A casual campaign bowling event
jokes.punchline: Tom has gone full fashion-statement, treating a casual bowling night as a runway opportunity
jokes.explanation: Standard Tom Haverford vanity joke. Gets the laugh from visual commitment. 'When you do it, you really do it' from Ben is the verbal punchline. Solid but not inventive — this is well within expected Tom territory.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Alright everyone, let's get this party started! I'm gonna drop some sick beats and show you how we do it in the Gergich household.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo! Who's ready to get jiggy with it? I've been practicing my dance moves all week.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I even bought this backwards baseball cap to show I'm hip to the times. What do you think? Pretty radical, right?

jokes.text: Jerry almost gives his Social Security number to a phone scammer while fundraising for Leslie
jokes.setup: Jerry is making fundraising calls
jokes.punchline: He says 'I don't really know why you would need my Social Security number, but — well, yeah, no. You're right. I guess it couldn't hurt to give it to you. It's 210—'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant escalation of Jerry's haplessness. He moves from suspicion ('I don't really know why') to capitulation ('I guess it couldn't hurt') to action ('It's 210—') in the span of one sentence. The fact that he starts reciting it is the perfect punchline. This is above-average Jerry comedy because it has a clear comedic structure rather than just 'Jerry is unfortunate.'

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Hey everyone, I just got tickets to the community theater's production of Cats! Who wants to go?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: April's phone call ends with '[creepy voice] I'm calling from inside your house.' — earns $100 donation
jokes.setup: April is making fundraising calls with complete contempt for the process
jokes.punchline: She threatens the donor in a horror-movie voice and it works — she gets $100
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: (1) April's nihilistic approach to the task and (2) the absurd fact that it WORKS. The horror-movie voice is peak April Ludgate. The success of the threat as a fundraising technique is the comedic escalation that makes it great. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It can't be. Phone banking is the worst. You're calling strangers and trying to convince them to care about something they don't care about. It's like being a telemarketer, except nobody hangs up on telemarketers because they're hoping to win a cruise.

jokes.text: Tom raps/sings an improvised song coaching April on the phone: '* COME ON NOW GET SOME MONEY * COME ON APRIL GET AN EARPIECE *'
jokes.setup: Tom is competitive about winning the movie tickets
jokes.punchline: He spontaneously coaches April through improvised rap while she's on a call
jokes.explanation: Fun moment but relies heavily on performance. The lyrics are banal ('get an earpiece' as rhyme content). Works as ensemble energy but isn't strong on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No one was thinking that.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was.

jokes.text: 'I don't care about that prize, but I'm gonna win because I want his happiness to go away.'
jokes.setup: April appears not to care about the movie ticket prize
jokes.punchline: She reveals her true motivation: not prizes, not Leslie's campaign, but the extinguishing of Tom's joy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I want his happiness to go away' is a perfectly April-coded expression of competitive spite — it's not even about winning for herself, it's about ending Tom's happiness as a goal in itself. The construction is precise and highly quotable. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm giving away two free movie tickets!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Two movie tickets? That's literally the best prize I've ever heard of. I'm going to see a film. In a theater. With a seat. This is incredible.

jokes.text: Tom cycles through increasingly absurd bowling name options: 'T Rex,' 'T-Boz,' 'Tommy Tsunami,' 'Ticky Ticky Tom-Tom,' 'Fly Guy' — Ann writes 'Tom'
jokes.setup: Tom needs a bowling nickname entered on the scoreboard
jokes.punchline: He rejects five elaborate options; Ann simply enters 'Tom'; he accepts it as 'Classic. Timeless.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of the names ('Ticky Ticky Tom-Tom') followed by Ann's pragmatic deflation and Tom's sincere approval of 'Classic. Timeless.' is a well-structured comedic sequence. The reversal — expecting him to reject 'Tom' and instead embrace it — is the satisfying punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I need to remain completely impartial as city manager. I can't show favoritism to any department.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That said, Parks and Recreation is clearly the best department in this city by a wide margin.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: In fact, I'd say they're the greatest municipal employees in the history of local government. They're like superheroes, but better because they're real. And so humble! So incredibly humble!

jokes.text: Leslie sends Derek a 'weird invitation' to the bowling event — she tracked him down from the focus group and specifically invited him
jokes.setup: Ben expresses surprise seeing Derek at the event; Leslie claims innocence
jokes.punchline: Derek confirms he got 'a weird invitation in the mail' — revealing Leslie did exactly what Ben told her not to do
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Leslie's earlier research. The 'weird invitation' framing confirms the audience's suspicion that Leslie orchestrated Derek's presence. The reveal through Derek's own mouth rather than Leslie admitting it is good structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Do I look laid-back?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You look... approachable.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I wouldn't know. I'm never on the other side of the glass with those things.' — Leslie lying directly to Derek's face with a straight expression
jokes.setup: Derek recognizes Leslie as the woman from the focus group
jokes.punchline: Leslie denies it with the specific technical phrasing of someone who is 100% absolutely on the other side of the glass
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'I'm never on the other side of the glass with those things' is perfect — it's technically true in the most lawyerly sense imaginable. She WAS on the other side of the glass watching him. The confident wrongness of the denial is great Leslie comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea why anyone comes to a bowling alley for the food. If I want a hot dog wrapped in a pizza, I'll just ask my wife to stop loving me.

jokes.text: Ron describes his bowling philosophy: 'Straight down the middle. No hook, no spin, no fuss. Anything more and this becomes figure skating.'
jokes.setup: Ron steps up to bowl
jokes.punchline: He equates any stylistic flourish in bowling with the effeminacy (to him) of figure skating — maximum masculine austerity applied to a leisure activity
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Ron Swanson character comedy. The figure skating comparison is unexpected and perfectly calibrated to his worldview — any unnecessary ornamentation is emasculating, even in bowling. 'Anything more and this becomes figure skating' is a great quotable line that illuminates his character perfectly. Only Ron would say this.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, are you scared to eat at the bowling alley?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Scared? No. I'm not scared of the bowling alley. The bowling alley is scared of me.

jokes.text: Ron talks to his bowling ball as if it's a large animal: 'Come on, big girl. Let's knock these little pins down.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just explained his austere, no-nonsense bowling philosophy
jokes.punchline: He immediately addresses his bowling ball as a large female animal with gentle authority, treating the pins as prey
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic inversion — Ron just declared no-fuss bowling and immediately has an intimate relationship with his ball that he names 'big girl.' The predatory framing of 'knock these little pins down' as a hunting metaphor is pure Ron. The juxtaposition with his previous speech is what makes it great.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hi, yes, I'm calling to see if you'd like to make a donation to the Parks Department. Who am I speaking with? Deirdre Splatterfork? Oh my God. Oh my God! That is the most beautiful name I have ever heard in my entire life. Deirdre Splatterfork. It's like a Tolkien character married a kitchen utensil. I'm in love with you.

jokes.text: 'Oh, my God, are you serious?' / 'Son, people can see you.' — Ron reacts to someone's bowling form or celebration
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Tom) bowls or celebrates in an elaborate way Ron finds embarrassing
jokes.punchline: 'Son, people can see you' — Ron's paternal disappointment expressed through concern for public visibility rather than the act itself
jokes.explanation: 'Son, people can see you' is a great Ron line — the paternal register and the implied shame of being observed are perfectly Ron. The economy is excellent. Without seeing the visual it's responding to, the line still works because it conjures the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Hello, yes, this is Jerry Gergich. Yes, G-E-R-G-I-C-H. My address? 1247 Elm Street, Pawnee, Indiana. My social security number? Sure, it's 043-29-1847. You need my mother's maiden name? That's Garfunkel. My PIN? It's 1234. Wait, should I not be giving you this information?

jokes.text: Tom's strike celebration — 'BOOM! That right there — Tommy's strike.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been performing his bowling persona all episode
jokes.punchline: Over-the-top self-congratulation for a routine bowling strike
jokes.explanation: Functional Tom vanity joke but not distinctive. Relies on character performance more than writing. 'Tommy's strike' in third person is mild.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to make a donation so large and so public that everyone will know I'm generous and thoughtful.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Just kidding, I'm going to donate nothing and tell everyone it was your idea to ask me.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's like that scene in The Ring where the girl has seven days to live. Except you have seven days to find another donor, and if you don't, you die. Metaphorically. Your event dies.

jokes.text: Derek asks if Leslie has scoliosis because of how she's standing while trying to look casual
jokes.setup: Leslie is performing 'being cas' (casual) with an awkward physical stance
jokes.punchline: Derek, not recognizing her performance, asks if she has a medical condition
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the earlier standing bit. Derek's sincere medical concern is the punchline — he genuinely can't tell her casual posture from a spinal condition. 'Oh no, I'm just being cas' as her response is good.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo! We just crushed that fundraising goal! That's what I'm talking about!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Tom Haverford in the house! Dropping knowledge, dropping dollars, dropping beats!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm the fundraising king, the money-making thing, hear my cash register cha-ching!

jokes.text: 'Damn it.' — Leslie bowls a strike but scolds herself because she was supposed to lose
jokes.setup: Leslie planned to lose intentionally to make Derek feel good; she bowls a strike
jokes.punchline: She reacts to her own success with frustration because it violates her tactical plan
jokes.explanation: The callback is tight. 'Damn it' is perfectly economical — we know exactly why she's upset, and Derek's confused 'Why are you mad? You bowled a strike' sets up her cover story perfectly. The cover ('that's how I motivate myself, never good enough') is also funny in its own right as an improv lie.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm only doing this because I want to win and have it be really obvious that I won, so that everyone knows that I'm better than them.

jokes.text: 'These beers are as cold as the Tuktoyaktuk Winter Road.' — Leslie's specific Ice Road Truckers reference to bond with Derek
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to find common ground with Derek over beer
jokes.punchline: She reaches for a hyper-specific Canadian ice road as a beer-temperature comparison, revealing she has done extensive research on Derek's TV preferences
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Tuktoyaktuk Winter Road' is doing all the work here. Leslie has clearly researched Derek's TV habits (alongside his bowling average) and is deploying this knowledge as a bonding tactic. The absurdly specific reference dressed as a casual beer comment is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, what about 'The Gutter King'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no... 'Strikes of Our Lives'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How about 'Tparker Posey'? Wait, that's taken.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What if I go by 'The Bowling Inferno'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 'Bowlzart' — Mozart, but bowling.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, I got it: 'Sir Bowls-a-Lot, Duke of Strikeonia, Protector of the Pins.'

jokes.text: 'Tom, I'm asking you as a man to stop this immediately.'
jokes.setup: Tom is doing something embarrassing (likely dancing or excessive celebration) at the bowling alley
jokes.punchline: Ron frames his request in terms of masculine honor — 'as a man' — implying Tom is doing something that violates the code
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'as a man' elevates this beyond a simple Ron disapproval beat — it implies a tribunal of manhood has deliberated and Tom is failing it. Good economy and character integration. Ron's disappointment is maximally expressed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What about 'T-Dawg'? Or 'Tommy Tubular'? 'The Tomster'? 'T-Money'?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No one cares.

jokes.text: 'BOOM!' / 'What the [bleep]?' — Tom's strike followed by a shocked reaction from someone nearby
jokes.setup: Tom has been warned to stop whatever he was doing
jokes.punchline: He apparently does something so physically extreme at his strike that someone within earshot is genuinely alarmed
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy beat that relies almost entirely on the unseen visual. The censored reaction is functional but we can't score the physical element we can't see. Mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Your nickname is Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Tom? That's perfect. That's the best nickname I've ever heard. Tom. I love it. Thank you, Donna. This is amazing.

jokes.text: BOOM! / WHAT THE [bleep]? (Ron's unexpected strike/bowling reaction)
jokes.setup: Ron bowls with his minimalist philosophy
jokes.punchline: An implied dramatic strike or crash earns a shocked reaction (likely Ron's devastating accuracy surprises everyone)
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. The humor is implied from context — Ron's no-nonsense bowling style producing a spectacular result. Not especially innovative but serves the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Wait, weren't you at the focus group yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No. No, I wasn't.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: You were definitely there. You were very vocal about municipal parking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I think you have me confused with someone else. I've never even been to a focus group. I don't know what those are.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: You asked for a second helping of the snack mix.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That wasn't me. I'm very opposed to snack mix. On principle.

jokes.text: April uses a rapid-fire Spanish 'mira mira mira mira mira' to convince a donor, then Ben switches to a southern accent with a fake grandmother proverb: 'You can't eat the biscuits if you don't pay for the flour'
jokes.setup: Fundraising calls continue; April is trying to close a donation
jokes.punchline: Someone (likely Andy) overhears and contributes a nonsense folk wisdom proverb in a fake Southern accent as if this is a real piece of advice
jokes.explanation: The fake folk wisdom proverb is nicely absurdist — it sounds like it means something but upon inspection is just a transactional statement about biscuits. The Southern accent suggests Andy. The 'mira mira' rapid-fire opening is also funny as improvised salesmanship.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no use for your fancy techniques. Bowling is about one thing and one thing only: throwing a heavy ball down a wooden lane. Everything else is just noise.

jokes.text: NO, MIRA, MIRA, MIRA, MIRA, MIRA. IT'S, LIKE, WHATEVER YOU WANT. LIKE, $10. IT DON'T MATTER.
jokes.setup: April is doing campaign fundraising calls
jokes.punchline: April's pitch has evolved into casual street vernacular — 'mira mira' and 'it don't matter' — a completely unorthodox but apparently effective approach
jokes.explanation: April's fundraising style being completely chaotic and yet effective is good character comedy. The casual bilingual street code-switching is very April.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm just gonna be cool about this. Real casual.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what, bowling ball? You're not even that round.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your holes are weird and small, and frankly, I've seen better grip patterns on a basketball.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So good luck with that, you beautiful, stupid sphere.

jokes.text: Ben on a call: '...I just want to live in a world that's a better place, and your contribution will definitely help us get there, to the... [sighs] better-place world, Fred.'
jokes.setup: Ben is making fundraising calls and tries to inspire the donor with a vision
jokes.punchline: He loses his train of thought mid-sentence and lands on 'the better-place world, Fred' — a complete linguistic collapse delivered with defeated sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'Better-place world, Fred' is a great small joke. The structure is perfect — ambitious inspirational language collapses into tautological defeat. The sigh and then the recovery attempt that fails again ('better-place world') is well-written cringe. Ben trying very hard and failing is one of the episode's minor pleasures.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you see that?! I threw it so hard, I thought for sure... Oh my God, it went right in the gutter.

jokes.text: 'Man, move over, pins. There's a new sheriff in town. You are so down with strikes, they should call you Norma Rae.'
jokes.setup: Leslie bowls another strike while supposedly trying to lose
jokes.punchline: She celebrates with a movie reference (Norma Rae) that Derek doesn't recognize, which she then has to explain, deflating the moment
jokes.explanation: The Norma Rae reference is characteristically Leslie — obscure enough that Derek has no idea what she's talking about, and then she has to explain it ('It's a Sally Field movie about unions. Doesn't matter.') which kills the compliment. Good self-defeating enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm going to give you some advice that I wish someone had given me when I was your age. When you realize you're bad at something, stop doing it in public.

jokes.text: Derek tells Leslie 'It's your turn. Try not to break a nail.' / Leslie: 'Ah, classic Derek with the zings.'
jokes.setup: Derek makes a mild, dated sexist quip
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds by enthusiastically crediting it as 'classic Derek with the zings' — treating the lamest possible insult as witty banter to maintain the social performance
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Leslie is so committed to the social operation that she has to validate Derek's weak banter as if it's great. 'Classic Derek with the zings' is perfect Leslie — sincere, slightly patronizing, and trying too hard. The characterization of Derek's weak joke as 'zings' is the comic heart.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, why are you so obsessed with this one person?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because Ben, if you care about the big picture, you have to care about every individual picture that makes up that big picture. And if you don't care about the small pictures, then the big picture is just a bunch of small pictures you don't care about, which means you don't actually care about the big picture at all. So really, by obsessing over this one person, I'm caring about the big picture more than anyone.

jokes.text: Ben's bowling metaphor: 'When you're bowling, try not to fixate on just one pin.' / Leslie: 'I realize that, but I will knock down this pin, and then this pin will knock down all the other pins.'
jokes.setup: Ben approaches Leslie with a transparent metaphor about not fixating on Derek
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds with complete literal sincerity — she either doesn't get the metaphor or is deliberately refusing it — and describes exactly what she's doing with Derek as if it's a bowling strategy
jokes.explanation: The meta-irony is that Leslie's bowling strategy (one pin knocking down all the others) is exactly how she thinks about Derek (win Derek, Derek converts everyone else). She's either unconsciously brilliant or stubbornly literal. The double meaning works perfectly as both bowling advice and political strategy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I promise I'll treat Derek exactly like everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've created a color-coded spreadsheet tracking his coffee preferences, work patterns, and optimal moments for 'spontaneous' encounters. I'll casually mention his interests in group settings to boost his confidence, then subtly guide conversations toward topics where he'll shine. I'm also scheduling strategic compliments for Tuesdays and Thursdays when his mood typically dips.

jokes.text: Derek asks Leslie to get him a beer; she says 'I don't work here.' He hands her $20. Leslie: 'Classic Derek.'
jokes.setup: Derek has been casually treating the event as a service experience
jokes.punchline: He attempts to pay Leslie $20 as if she's a server; she takes it as more 'Derek zings' ('Classic Derek')
jokes.explanation: The 'Classic Derek' running gag is developing but the joke itself is thin. Derek's obliviousness is consistent characterization but the 'I don't work here' beat is predictable.

jokes.text: Chris announces he's going to ask Millicent to move in with him — mid-phone-bank, during a 'probiotic tea break' — then remembers to ask Jerry's permission as an afterthought
jokes.setup: Chris calls a probiotic tea break and has 'big news'
jokes.punchline: He announces moving in with Jerry's daughter, having already described the whole plan, then adds 'I mean, if that's okay with you of course, Jerry' — treating parental consent as a bureaucratic afterthought
jokes.explanation: The D.I.— caught mid-sentence correction ('D-I— I mean, if that's okay with you of course, Jerry') is a good tell — he almost says 'Done!' before catching himself. Chris's oblivious confidence applied to dating someone's daughter is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Do you have scoliosis?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, I'm just being ca-sual.

jokes.text: Chris reveals he wants to live in an octagonal house because 'an octagon is the optimal shape for a home in terms of energy flow'
jokes.setup: Chris is sharing real estate plans
jokes.punchline: An octagonal house for energy flow reasons — Chris applies his wellness pseudo-science to architecture
jokes.explanation: Solid Chris Traeger absurdism. He's applied his health optimization philosophy to home geometry. 'Optimal shape for energy flow' is exactly how Chris thinks about everything. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you love wings? I'm shocked. I thought you hated wings.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, no, that makes total sense. Of course you love wings.

jokes.text: 'Jerry, I love it when you pull rank.' — Chris's sincere response to Jerry's mild managerial request
jokes.setup: Jerry sheepishly asks Chris to take his break in the other room
jokes.punchline: Chris treats Jerry's tentative management as a bold power move he finds thrilling — which makes Jerry's pathetic attempt at authority more pathetic
jokes.explanation: Good joke that works in two directions: Chris is the only person who would find Jerry's mild request thrilling, and Jerry's 'rank' is so minimal that Chris's enthusiasm is absurd. Shows both characters well.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Why are you mad? You just bowled a strike.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I'm not supposed to be good at things! I'm supposed to be quirky and lovable and a little bit of a mess. My therapist says I have a fear of success because my dad never validated me, and my mom was too busy with her horses.

jokes.text: Ann whispers to Jerry that Millicent is going to break up with Chris, forcing Jerry to awkwardly pretend not to know while Chris is in earshot
jokes.setup: Chris has just enthusiastically announced moving in with Millicent
jokes.punchline: Ann drops the bomb that Millicent is definitely going to break up with him, creating immediate dramatic irony and Jerry's uncomfortable position
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is well-set-up — Chris's happiness is immediately undercut. The rewatch value is high because you know what's coming for Chris. Jerry's 'It's not my fault' when the blame comes is funny but hasn't happened yet.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Here you go, Derek. A nice cold beer.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Thanks, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, this beer is brewed in a small town in Belgium, right between where they make chocolate and where they make waffles.

jokes.text: Donna whispers that Millicent is going to break up with Chris; April and someone else confirm; they discuss it while Chris is right there
jokes.setup: Chris has just announced his big plan to ask Millicent to move in
jokes.punchline: Donna immediately tells the group that Millicent is going to dump him — discussed in whispers while Chris is nearby, oblivious and happy — the dramatic irony creates dark comedy
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony setup. The comedy of watching Chris be blissfully unaware while his friends know he's about to be dumped is dark but characteristic of the show's warm cruelty. Donna's certainty ('she is definitely gonna do it') is the confident delivery that sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Wait, is that a reference to something?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No. I mean, maybe. I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I watch lots of normal TV. Regular person TV.

jokes.text: 'Hey Ron. Were you trying to get a seven? Because if you were, you did a great job.'
jokes.setup: Ron has clearly gotten a bad result (only knocking down the seven-pin, or getting a 7)
jokes.punchline: Tom congratulates Ron for what is clearly a failure, framing it as an achievement
jokes.explanation: Decent ironic congratulations. Works because Tom is punching up at Ron for once. The delivery of 'you did a great job' as sincere praise for a failure is the comedic element. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, I know you're excited about your bowling score, but I need you to listen to me very carefully. You are a man. Act like one.

jokes.text: [whines] MY FINGER WAS IN THERE. RON CRUSHED MY FINGER. I THINK IT MIGHT BE BROKEN. / ARE YOU A FEMALE BIRD? / IT WAS AN ACCIDENT.
jokes.setup: Ron has apparently dropped or rolled a bowling ball and Tom's finger was in the ball holes
jokes.punchline: Tom whines at length; Ron's response is not sympathy but 'Are you a female bird?' — an insult meaning 'are you a hen/a whiner' — before flatly noting it was an accident
jokes.explanation: 'Are you a female bird?' is a spectacularly Ron Swanson insult — a euphemism for 'hen' (which sounds like whiner) delivered with total seriousness. It's unexpected, period-appropriate in its strangeness, and perfectly character-integrated. One of the episode's more memorable lines.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Did you see that? I think I just bowled a perfect game!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait... that ball just went straight into the gutter. How is that possible?

jokes.text: Tom's theatrical crying over Ron crushing his finger: 'RON CRUSHED MY FINGER. I THINK IT MIGHT BE BROKEN.' / Ron: 'Are you a female bird?' / Tom: 'You did this on purpose. You're jealous of my gift.'
jokes.setup: Ron has accidentally crushed Tom's finger with the bowling ball
jokes.punchline: Tom's disproportionate reaction ('I think it might be broken') prompts Ron's contemptuous 'Are you a female bird?' (i.e., a hen/tweety bird), then Tom's paranoid accusation that Ron is jealous of his gift
jokes.explanation: 'Are you a female bird?' is a great Ron insult — it's contemptuous of Tom's sensitivity while being oddly specific and therefore funny. 'You're jealous of my gift' as Tom's paranoid escalation is also good. The sequence has nice momentum.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm calling to ask if you'd like to donate to the Parks and Recreation Department. We do stuff like... maintain parks. And recreation. Anyway, it doesn't really matter if you donate or not. We'll probably be fine. Or we won't be. Either way, I'll still be here tomorrow doing this exact same thing.

jokes.text: 'Okay, come on, Tweety Bird, let's get you some ice.'
jokes.setup: Tom is whimpering about his injured finger
jokes.punchline: Ron has gone from contempt to a gruff paternal care — calling him 'Tweety Bird' while taking him for ice
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'female bird' with 'Tweety Bird' works well. Ron's grudging paternal care despite his contempt is a classic Ron-Tom dynamic beat. The nickname landing as affectionate after being contemptuous is the comic turn.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey there, friend! This is Andy Dwyer calling from the Parks Department, and boy oh boy, do I have a opportunity for you! You know what my pappy used to say? He said, 'Andy, money is just like a beautiful woman – you gotta treat it real nice or it'll run off with a banker.' Now that don't make no sense, but it sounds real good! So whatcha say, partner? You gonna help us out or are you gonna be one of them fancy city folk who don't care about parks?

jokes.text: Leslie asks Derek point-blank if she has his vote after their whole evening together. He says no. She does the 'chuckles Derek you old so-and-so' bit trying to laugh it off.
jokes.setup: After an entire evening of strategic socializing, Leslie asks the direct question
jokes.punchline: Derek's flat 'no' followed by Leslie's forced laugh and 'Derek, you old so-and-so' — treating his rejection as banter while clearly devastated
jokes.explanation: The cringe is well-constructed. Leslie's forced-banter response to a direct 'no' shows how desperately she's trying to maintain the social fiction. 'Derek, you old so-and-so' is a brilliantly pathetic response to rejection — it's what you say to a friend who teases you, not to someone who just said they won't vote for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hi Mrs. Henderson, this is Ben Wyatt calling from the Parks Department. We're raising funds for the new community center and I was wondering if you'd be interested in making a donation?

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Henderson
dialogue.line: Well, my husband and I have been having some issues lately.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm sorry to hear that, but maybe the community center could be a place where you two—

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Henderson
dialogue.line: He never listens to me. He's always on his phone. We haven't been intimate in months.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Um, I think you might need to talk to a professional about that.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Henderson
dialogue.line: You seem like a good listener, Ben. What do you think I should do?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I really think a marriage counselor would be better equipped to—

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Henderson
dialogue.line: Should I leave him?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm just trying to raise money for a community center.

jokes.text: Derek says 'I don't like you, okay?' flatly — the bluntest possible answer to why he won't vote for Leslie
jokes.setup: Leslie can't understand why Derek won't vote for her after their fun evening
jokes.punchline: 'I don't like you, okay?' — no policy reason, no bowling reason, just personal dislike delivered without ceremony
jokes.explanation: The brutal economy of 'I don't like you, okay?' after all of Leslie's elaborate wooing is perfectly timed. It deflates the entire operation in four words. The 'okay?' qualifier suggests Derek finds her persistence exhausting, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You know what? You're going to be great. You're going to be so great, you're going to be... great.

jokes.text: Leslie retaliates by confessing she pretended to lose and is actually a great bowler. Derek: 'Yeah, right. I destroyed you.' / Leslie: 'I am a really good bowler. Ask Ron.' / Derek: 'I don't know who Ron is.'
jokes.setup: Confrontation after Derek says he doesn't like her
jokes.punchline: The entire 'Ask Ron' running gag pays off as Leslie's only credential — she invokes Ron as the arbiter of her bowling skill to a stranger who has never met Ron, making the appeal completely useless
jokes.explanation: This is the best callback/running gag payoff in the episode. The 'Ask Ron' joke has been building since the cold open — it's been Leslie's go-to verification mechanism. Here, she deploys it against a man who has never met Ron, and Derek's flat 'I don't know who Ron is' destroys the appeal entirely. The joke works structurally (perfect callback payoff), character-wise (Leslie's blind faith in Ron as universal authority), and emotionally (she has nothing else to offer). The structure from setup to payoff is genuinely excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Derek, that was an amazing bowling performance. You really knocked it out of the park. Or should I say, you knocked the pins out of the... pins place. You're like the LeBron James of bowling, if LeBron James bowled. Which he probably does. Do you think LeBron bowls?

jokes.text: 'I'd like to introduce you to my good friend, Anyone Else.' / Leslie: 'Not now, Ben. I'd like to introduce Derek's ass to my foot.'
jokes.setup: Ben tries to redirect Leslie's attention away from Derek
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response escalates from 'Not now' to a declaration of physical vengeance on Derek in the same breath
jokes.explanation: The structure is good: Ben's introduction of 'Anyone Else' as a person is a playful framing of a serious request; Leslie immediately rejects both the playfulness and the seriousness with her counter-declaration. 'Introduce Derek's ass to my foot' is a funny threat that also reveals how far off the rails she's gone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Norma Rae is this classic film from 1979 about a working-class woman in North Carolina who stands up to her employer and becomes a labor activist. It's incredibly inspiring and Sally Field won an Oscar for her performance. It's a really important movie about workers' rights and—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what, never mind, it doesn't matter.

jokes.text: Ben and Ann awkward silence / Champion the three-legged dog is used as an excuse to escape awkward situation: 'What, Champion? You need to go outside now? Come on. That a boy. Sorry, he's — hates awkward situations.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Ann have an uncomfortable moment — likely because of the developing romantic tension or knowledge they both share about Chris
jokes.punchline: Ben uses Champion (who can't speak) as a ventriloquist excuse to escape, then explains 'he hates awkward situations' — projecting his own feelings onto the dog
jokes.explanation: 'He hates awkward situations' is a great line because it's obviously Ben projecting. Using a dog to escape a human social situation is relatable and Ben-appropriate. The three-legged dog detail (Champion) adds a visual element that makes the escape more absurd.

jokes.text: 'Terrible moonwalk.' / 'Don't care.'
jokes.setup: Tom (or someone) attempts a moonwalk celebration after a good bowl
jokes.punchline: Ben's flat assessment ('terrible moonwalk') is met with Tom's equally flat indifference ('don't care')
jokes.explanation: Four words, two characters, two perspectives perfectly expressed. The economy is exceptional. The exchange captures the Ben/Tom dynamic — Ben's critical assessment and Tom's complete self-confidence — in the most minimal possible form.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, wow! That was a real zinger, Derek! You really got me there!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Sexism is hilarious!

jokes.text: TERRIBLE MOONWALK. / DON'T CARE.
jokes.setup: Leslie apparently does a moonwalk to celebrate her bowling
jokes.punchline: Ben critiques the technical execution; Leslie's 'Don't care' is the perfect response
jokes.explanation: Two words, perfect joke. The humor is layered: Leslie is doing a moonwalk in a bowling alley as a celebration, Ben feels the need to critique its technical quality, and Leslie's 'Don't care' is the ideal rejoinder — she's not trying to do a good moonwalk, she's just living in the moment. Exceptional economy. Rewatch bonus because the visual is presumably hilarious.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Don't fixate on one pin. You gotta see the whole lane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's actually genius advice for campaign strategy. Don't fixate on one demographic—see the whole electorate.

jokes.text: 'Aw, you got a spare. That's so cute.' — Leslie to Derek, condescendingly, after she's abandoned the plan to lose intentionally
jokes.setup: Leslie has abandoned her plan to lose; Derek gets a spare
jokes.punchline: Leslie's condescending 'that's so cute' — treating a spare as a child's achievement — reveals how completely she's dropped the political performance and entered competitive mode
jokes.explanation: Great character moment. This single line shows Leslie has completely abandoned the political mission and entered pure competitor mode. 'That's so cute' as athletic trash talk is perfectly Leslie — it's condescending, it's competitive, and it's the exact opposite of what she planned to do.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Hey Ben, get me a beer.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not a waiter, Derek. I work in government.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Yeah, so get me a beer.

jokes.text: Donna tells Chris 'you might want to take a jacket, it's about to get cold out there' / Chris: 'Thanks, Donna, but Millicent's company will keep me warm.' / Donna: 'Take the jacket.'
jokes.setup: Chris is going for a stroll with Millicent
jokes.punchline: Donna's ominous jacket advice is a metaphor for the imminent breakup; Chris takes it literally and refuses; Donna simply repeats 'Take the jacket' — she knows what's coming
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy construction. The double meaning of 'it's about to get cold out there' works perfectly — literal weather, metaphorical heartbreak. Chris's cheerful refusal ('Millicent's company will keep me warm') is dramatic irony at its best, and Donna's flat 'Take the jacket' as a final warning is perfectly timed. The economy is excellent and the structure is tight. Strong candidate for standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Derek, Ben works here now. He's part of the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Wait, Ben? Your husband Ben?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! And it's great because now we get to spend all day together doing what we love — public service!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We actually try to avoid each other during work hours.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But when we do see each other, it's super romantic. We once made eye contact by the vending machine. Very charming.

jokes.text: 'I wished for his happiness to go away. I might be a wizard.'
jokes.setup: April declared she wanted Tom's happiness to go away; Chris is now going to get his heart broken
jokes.punchline: April attributes Chris's impending heartbreak to her own wish for Tom's happiness to end — and entertains the possibility she has magical powers
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke of the episode and one of the best April Ludgate lines in the series. It's a perfect callback: her earlier stated wish to extinguish Tom's happiness has accidentally manifested against CHRIS (wrong person), and rather than feeling bad, she considers whether she has wizard powers. The dark self-absorption, the confused logic, the complete lack of empathy for Chris, and the sincerity of 'I might be a wizard' — all of this is peak April. It's quotable, character-specific, structurally perfect (callback + escalation + absurdism), and gets a huge laugh. This approaches the Snip-Snap calibration zone in terms of character comedy execution.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I wanted to ask Jerry for his blessing before I proposed to Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My blessing?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I wanted to ask Ann's father for his blessing.

jokes.text: HEY, DEREK. WHAT A DEFEAT, MAN. I MEAN, I DID NOT EXPECT TO WIN BY THAT MUCH.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just beaten Derek convincingly at bowling
jokes.punchline: She frames her sportsmanship as congratulating him on 'his defeat' and expresses false modesty about the margin of victory
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie victory lap moment. Congratulating someone on their 'defeat' (rather than your win) is a classic Leslie formulation — technically gracious, functionally devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Octagonal houses are statistically proven to have 12% fewer negative energy vortexes. It's science.

jokes.text: 'Oh, look. Here's that photo op you wanted.' — Ben to Leslie after the punch
jokes.setup: The bowling event was designed to be a good photo op for Leslie's campaign
jokes.punchline: Ben, having just punched a focus group participant, sardonically notes that THIS is the photo op they'll get
jokes.explanation: Strong callback that earns its score. The photo op was discussed as a political asset; now it will be a liability. Ben's ability to land a perfect deadpan line immediately after throwing a punch at a voter is both funny and shows character — he's already in damage-control mode. The irony lands hard.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Why don't you take your break in the living room?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's a great idea, Jerry. You're really thinking outside the box here. This is the kind of initiative that gets people promoted.

jokes.text: Leslie imitates gunfire sounds while recapping events to Ben/camera, then: 'What's wrong with you?' / 'I don't know, I just — I have a lot of adrenaline right now.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is processing what just happened
jokes.punchline: Her attempt to recount events devolves into gunfire sound effects; when called out she attributes it to adrenaline
jokes.explanation: Leslie's adrenaline-addled recap is good character comedy — she's so excited by Ben's act of chivalry that her verbal processing breaks down. The gunfire sounds are unexpected and funny. 'I have a lot of adrenaline right now' is a good small punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm so excited about moving in with you, Chris. I've never lived with anyone before.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, you're going to love it. We'll have so much fun together.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know. I've been practicing my roommate skills. I alphabetized your spice rack and color-coded your socks by shade and thread count.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Jerry, that's... a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: (whispering) I also replaced all your regular light bulbs with full-spectrum ones so you'd have better mood lighting. And I laminated a chore chart.

jokes.text: Leslie says 'What Ben did was warranted and extremely awesome, by the way. Did you write down how awesome it was?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is talking to a police officer/Randy about pressing charges
jokes.punchline: She advocates for Ben's assault and asks the officer to note its awesomeness in the official record
jokes.explanation: 'Did you write down how awesome it was?' directed at a police officer is a great Leslie Knope line — bureaucratically minded even in chaos, wanting official documentation of awesomeness. The officer's response ('we refrain from using words like jerk or awesome') is the perfect deadpan callback to institutional language.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm very angry.

jokes.text: 'Wow, you and me, huh? Hurt fingies.' — Ben to Tom, both injured, attempting camaraderie
jokes.setup: Ben has hurt his hand punching Derek; Tom has his finger injury from earlier
jokes.punchline: Ben attempts a bonding moment over shared injury using the word 'fingies' — which is extremely un-Ben
jokes.explanation: Ben using the baby-talk 'fingies' is funny because it's so out of character — he's clearly still adrenaline-charged. Tom's response ('No, no, two totally different injuries') immediately hierarchizing the injuries is good secondary comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have sustained a devastating injury to my bowling wrist. This is serious. I may never bowl again. My career in casual recreational sports is over.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You bowled one frame.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: One frame! That's all it takes. One frame to change your life forever.

jokes.text: 'No, no, two totally different injuries.' — Tom refusing to accept equivalence between his finger injury and Ben's punching hand
jokes.setup: Ben tries to commiserate over their matching injuries
jokes.punchline: Tom insists his injury is categorically different — implicitly claiming his is more serious or more legitimate
jokes.explanation: Good small joke from Tom's vanity. He can't let Ben's punch injury share status with his Ron-induced finger crushing. Tom's need to have the most significant injury is in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why are you still talking?

jokes.text: Ann and Jerry learn Chris is getting broken up with; Ann says 'Damn you, Jerry' / Jerry: 'It's not my fault'
jokes.setup: Chris reports the breakup; the group reacts
jokes.punchline: Ann instinctively blames Jerry for the breakup that has nothing to do with him; Jerry's helpless 'It's not my fault' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Standard Jerry-as-scapegoat joke. Works because of how reflexive Ann's blame is — there's no logic to it, but the instinct is there. 'It's not my fault' as Jerry's entirely reasonable defense makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I know what this is about. You're jealous because I bowled a 147 and you've never broken 100.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, I don't care about your bowling score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's exactly what someone who's jealous would say.

jokes.text: April wins the fundraising competition; Andy says 'Yes! That's my wife.'
jokes.setup: The winner of the fundraising competition is announced
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate proud spousal claim — he had nothing to do with April's win but claims ownership of her achievement with pure enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Andy's pride is completely in character — simple, pure, enthusiastic. 'That's my wife' is the Andy equivalent of a trophy. Works as a sweet callback to April's sinister competitive motivation.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, you're like a bird that's been shot. You just keep flying in circles, getting worse.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not helping, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to help. I'm trying to describe what I'm witnessing.

jokes.text: Ben bowls one-handed with an injured punching hand, gets a strike, then: 'King Kong ain't got nothing on me. Ow, my fingie still hurts.'
jokes.setup: Ben is pressured to bowl despite his injured hand
jokes.punchline: He bowls a strike one-handed, delivers an absurdly confident movie quote, and immediately deflates himself with 'Ow, my fingie still hurts'
jokes.explanation: The transition from 'King Kong ain't got nothing on me' (Training Day reference, peak bravado) to 'Ow, my fingie still hurts' (immediate physical vulnerability using the baby-talk word) is a perfect comedic deflation. The callback of 'fingie' from Ben's earlier usage is also good.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Derek, I'm just gonna level with you. I need your vote. What do you say? You gonna help me out? We cool? That's tight. Fo' shizzle?

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: ...What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I said fo' shizzle. It means 'for sure.' I'm hip. I'm with it.

jokes.text: 'Oh, the bravery. The perseverance. You're an American hero.' — Leslie to Ben after his one-handed strike
jokes.setup: Ben bowls a strike one-handed
jokes.punchline: Leslie delivers escalating heroic language for bowling, culminating in 'American hero' — a phrase that usually requires more than bowling
jokes.explanation: Leslie's hyperbolic sincerity applied to minor athletic achievements is characteristic. The escalating praise ('bravery,' 'perseverance,' 'American hero') applied to a bowling strike is good. It also carries the subtext that she's genuinely thrilled with Ben, which adds warmth.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: Look, I appreciate what you're doing for the parks, but you're not getting my vote. Honestly, you're kind of annoying. You talk too much, you're always trying too hard, and you make me uncomfortable.

jokes.text: The newspaper headline Ben proposes: 'No-Strike-Bowling Bowler Struck by Knope's Striking Beau'
jokes.setup: Ben references the photo op / newspaper coverage of his punching Derek
jokes.punchline: A headline that packs three different meanings of 'strike' into one sentence (bowling, assault, impressive), while also calling himself 'beau' — journalistically and romantically self-referential
jokes.explanation: This is clever wordplay that earns its high score: the triple meaning of 'strike' (bowling strike, striking someone, striking/impressive), the formal newspaper-headline register, and Ben calling himself 'beau' with complete self-awareness. The construction is genuinely impressive — this is writing room wordplay that rewards attention. Strong candidate for standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm actually really good at bowling. I have a 147 average.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: That's not even a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It is! A 147 average means I bowl a 147 on average!

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: No one has ever bowled a 147.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have! Multiple times! Why won't you believe me?

jokes.text: 'Not today. I don't deserve it.' — Leslie refusing whipped cream as self-punishment for the Derek fiasco
jokes.setup: Ben offers Leslie whipped cream (apparently a comfort ritual) during the press conference prep
jokes.punchline: 'Not today. I don't deserve it.' — treating whipped cream as a reward to be earned
jokes.explanation: 'I don't deserve it' applied to whipped cream is peak Leslie Knope — she has a childhood comfort food that she has apparently made a moral reward system around. The economy is perfect and the character integration is excellent. Only Leslie would have whipped cream as both a comfort and a merit-based privilege.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I need your advice on something.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm listening.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you think I should do about this situation?

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: I don't care what Ron thinks.

jokes.text: LET ME RESIGN. IT'S THE ONLY THING THAT TRULY PROTECTS YOU. / NON-STARTER.
jokes.setup: Ben is offering to resign as campaign manager to protect Leslie from political fallout
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate 'Non-starter' dismisses the idea without discussion — she won't entertain it for a moment
jokes.explanation: Leslie's loyalty expressed in one crisp word. 'Non-starter' is exactly the language Leslie would use in a governing context deployed here for a personal/romantic declaration. Economy and character integration are the strengths.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Everyone, this is Derek. He's... here.

jokes.text: 'But this is ridiculous. I do need more whipped cream. Ma'am.'
jokes.setup: Leslie denied herself whipped cream; then she talks about the absurdity of the situation
jokes.punchline: She reverses her whipped cream ban mid-sentence and flags down a server — the crisis of self-denial lasts approximately ninety seconds
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The reversal is fast (under two minutes of screen time) and the punchline — calling 'Ma'am' to a server mid-confessional — is perfectly timed. It shows Leslie can't maintain self-denial for long when whipped cream is available. The 'Ma'am' as the final word of the turn is great.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, Leslie, I'd like to introduce you to the concept of irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, Ben, I'd like to introduce you to the concept of shut your mouth.

jokes.text: BUT THIS IS RIDICULOUS. I DO NEED MORE WHIPPED CREAM. MA'AM.
jokes.setup: Leslie had declared she doesn't deserve whipped cream as punishment
jokes.punchline: Thirty seconds later, she reverses her position and summons a server
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback button. The joke of 'I don't deserve it' is funny on its own; the callback of 'this is ridiculous, I DO need more whipped cream' thirty seconds later is even better. It's a tiny character arc compressed into two beats, and the mid-sentence pivot from serious self-examination to 'Ma'am' (summoning service) is impeccably timed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for the twenty dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? For someone like you, I could set you up with a platinum package. That's only four hundred and ninety-five dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Or, if you're really serious about this, we have our diamond level, which is twenty-five hundred.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That gets you a custom leather portfolio, a pen that costs more than your car, and my personal cell phone number so you can call me whenever you want business advice.

jokes.text: April's confessional: Chris announces his breakup news with 'here's why it may be the greatest thing that ever happened' — April's reaction beat: dead stare, then 'Yeah, good point. Hadn't thought about it that way. Um, here.' [hands him movie tickets]
jokes.setup: Chris has just been broken up with but is spinning it as a positive development with a long explanation
jokes.punchline: April's completely hollow validation ('Good point. Hadn't thought about it that way.') followed by giving him the movie tickets as a mercy gesture — the entire exchange is April pretending to engage with Chris's emotional monologue
jokes.explanation: The joke is April's complete emotional absence — she clearly didn't listen to a word Chris said but delivers 'Yeah, good point, hadn't thought about it that way' as a conversation-ending courtesy. Then giving him the movie tickets is a small act of genuine kindness from someone who won't admit to having feelings. The deadpan and the tiny warmth are perfectly balanced. Strong April character work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, so... I should probably go. My dog is really upset about something.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I can tell because he's making that face where he's mad at me.

jokes.text: 'There are three of them. I thought there were only two.' / April: 'Yeah, I know, I bought another one because I thought maybe you, me, and Andy could go to the movies sometime.' / 'Just take the stupid tickets. I'm just trying to be nice.'
jokes.setup: April gives Chris two movie tickets as a gesture; he notices there are three
jokes.punchline: April bought a third ticket because she wanted to invite him to a group outing — then immediately undercuts the kindness with 'Just take the stupid tickets. I'm just trying to be nice.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most emotionally rich comedy moments. The reveal that April bought a third ticket for Chris (completely unnecessary, she just won two) is a surprise act of kindness from the least sentimental character on the show. Then she immediately dismantles it with 'Just take the stupid tickets. I'm just trying to be nice.' — the embarrassment of being caught being kind is perfectly April. The character integration is near-perfect: 9.5. This moment is both funny and genuinely touching.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the worst moonwalk I've ever seen. Michael Jackson is rolling in his grave. Probably moonwalking.

jokes.text: Leslie at press conference: 'I'd like to first start by saying thank you for coming. And on behalf of Ben Wyatt and everyone involved in my campaign, I'm very sorry for what happened... You know what? No. I'm not.'
jokes.setup: Leslie begins a prepared, professional apology at a press conference
jokes.punchline: Mid-apology, she aborts, reverses course, and says 'I'm not sorry' — the carefully staged event collapses in real time
jokes.explanation: The reversal is perfectly timed and executed. The comedy is in watching Leslie's political instincts ('thank you for coming,' formal third-person reference to Ben Wyatt) immediately collapse under the weight of her actual feelings. The 'You know what? No. I'm not.' mid-apology is great structure. This is Leslie at her best — authentic over strategic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you're talking about. A song is a song. If it's catchy, it's good. That's it. That's the whole thing.

jokes.text: Leslie's press conference: 'I'm very sorry for what happened... You know what? No, I'm not.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is at a damage-control press conference, trying to apologize
jokes.punchline: She begins a standard political non-apology, then pivots mid-sentence to full honesty — abandoning the script entirely
jokes.explanation: One of Leslie's best moments in the episode. The political non-apology setup is subverted when she abandons it mid-clause. 'You know what? No, I'm not.' is a great punchline because it's simultaneously bad politics and great character — it's Leslie being authentic even when authenticity is strategically terrible. The structure (fake apology → genuine defiance) is textbook misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ha! In your face! I am the bowling champion! I am the queen of the lanes! Bow before me, peasants!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're being really unsportsmanlike right now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't care! I won fair and square, and now I get to rub it in all of your faces for the rest of eternity!

jokes.text: Leslie admits at the press conference that after Derek was punched, 'my campaign manager and I made out a lot afterward. Ah, I probably shouldn't have said that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has abandoned the script and is now confessing to the press conference what actually happened
jokes.punchline: She includes 'we made out a lot' as a relevant fact about the evening, then immediately recognizes this was a mistake
jokes.explanation: 'I probably shouldn't have said that' as the self-correction after 'we made out a lot' is perfect Leslie — she's been increasingly honest and the overshare is the logical endpoint. The juxtaposition of professional press conference language with 'made out a lot' is excellent. The belated recognition ('I probably shouldn't have said that') rather than an immediate catch makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Derek, that's amazing! You got a strike! Well, technically it's a spare, but for you, that might as well be a strike. I'm so proud of you!

jokes.text: 'But you should be warned. If you do not vote for me, my boyfriend might beat you up.' — Leslie, at a press conference, as her closing statement
jokes.setup: Leslie is wrapping up her unconventional press conference non-apology
jokes.punchline: She closes with what is effectively a physical threat to voters — framed with the conditional and the boyfriend qualifier as if this is a reasonable campaign message
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. The structure is perfect — she ends the anti-apology not with a policy statement but with a semi-joking threat, framed with enough deniability ('might beat you up') that she can almost pretend it's not a threat. 'My boyfriend might beat you up' as a campaign promise is absurdist and deeply Leslie. The 'might' is doing critical work — it's both threatening and legally defensible. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have the ability to sense when people are about to receive bad news. I'm sensing it right now. You're about to get bad news.

jokes.text: Derek tells Leslie she's being 'kind of a bitch right now' at her own press conference — Leslie: 'See? So I'm not going to apologize.'
jokes.setup: Derek is at the press conference and contributes his assessment
jokes.punchline: Leslie uses Derek's real-time inappropriate outburst as evidence that she was right not to apologize — he's proving her point for her
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: Derek is there, he says the slur again in a more public setting, and Leslie immediately incorporates it into her argument. 'See?' as a pivot is perfect. Derek's presence at the press conference and his repeated behavior is both absurd and the perfect demonstration of Leslie's thesis.

jokes.text: Second focus group after the press conference debacle: people now like Leslie because 'I like that one guy punched the other guy, and she stood by him.'
jokes.setup: The first focus group gave mixed responses; now after the punch and the non-apology press conference, a second group is assembled
jokes.punchline: The visceral, chaotic response (guy punched guy; she stood by him) has improved her numbers — 'people vote with their gut' pays off literally
jokes.explanation: The callback to the episode's central theme ('people vote with their gut') pays off perfectly here. The reason voters now like her has nothing to do with policy — it's that her boyfriend punched a jerk and she didn't apologize. The irony that chaos improved her image is the episode's thematic punchline, executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That was amazing! Ben, you just punched Derek! I've never been more attracted to you!

jokes.text: 'Yeah, that guy said he didn't like my earrings. Go punch him.' — focus group participant to Ben
jokes.setup: A focus group participant is encouraged by the punching precedent
jokes.punchline: She immediately requests a punch on her behalf for a petty personal slight
jokes.explanation: Great joke that escalates the absurdity of the focus group discovering punching as political currency. 'Go punch him' delivered as a genuine campaign request is funny and captures Pawnee's unique civic culture. Ben's response 'Sure' (implied) completing the bit is the perfect beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Pew pew! Pew pew pew!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm just... practicing my gun sounds for the Sweetums presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: By making them right now? In the middle of the office?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Would you rather I do it unprepared?

jokes.text: Ron uses the wrong bowling lane — takes the ball all the way to Lane 22 at the 'very end' — then: 'Son of a bitch.' [grunting for 15+ seconds]
jokes.setup: Ron is sent to Lane 8 but insists on Lane 22
jokes.punchline: Extended grunting/physical effort implied by 15 seconds of transcript silence and 'son of a bitch' as the establishing line — Ron is doing something extreme with a bowling ball alone at the end of the alley
jokes.explanation: This is a great Ron Swanson visual/physical gag. He demands the remotest lane for privacy, and then whatever he does is apparently so extreme that it takes sustained effort and produces 'son of a bitch.' The mystery of what Ron is actually doing (bowling multiple balls? extreme technique? rage at his earlier bad score?) is funnier than anything explicit. Character integration is exceptional — only Ron would go this far alone for bowling privacy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Let's just put down that Ben was 'aggressively volunteering' and Derek got in the way of his fist.

jokes.text: 'Hey, perfect game. What's your name? Put it up on a wall.' / Ron: 'I was never here, and you will never speak of this again.'
jokes.setup: Ron has apparently bowled a perfect game alone in Lane 22
jokes.punchline: 'I was never here, and you will never speak of this again.' — Ron refuses public recognition of his achievement and demands complete secrecy
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest closing joke and earns its high score on every dimension. Ron bowled a perfect game in total secrecy, refused to share it with anyone, and upon being discovered demands a cone of silence. The character integration is perfect (10): Ron's self-sufficient excellence that requires no audience is his defining trait. The structure is perfect: the setup (Lane 22, grunting, isolation) pays off with the perfect game revelation, and the punchline ('I was never here') is the maximum expression of Ron Swanson's philosophy. It's comparable to 'when I eat, it is the food that is scared' in terms of Ron-character encapsulation. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey buddy, how ya doing? You feeling okay? You need anything? Water? Juice? A little snack?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm fine. It's just a minor injury.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, so you think you're tough? Let me tell you something — I am also injured. We're injury buddies now. We're bonded for life.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Does somebody need a boo-boo kiss?

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben host a bowling night after receiving feedback about Leslie's campaign. April, Chris, and Jerry hold a competition to see who can raise the most funds.
insight: Campaign chaos hits 105 jokes, but 72-score reveals pacing struggle with cringe.
